The geodesic dome is an architectural structure composed of triangular panels arranged over a sphere or hemisphere, designed to span large distances while minimizing material and weight. Invented by Buckminster Fuller in the nineteen fifties, it became an icon of space-age optimism and experimental design, combining elegant geometry with practical efficiency.

The geodesic dome is constructed from a framework of triangles connected at vertices—this distribution of stress across many points allows the structure to be both lightweight and strong. Fuller's insight was that a dome following geodesic lines—the shortest paths on a sphere—would maximize strength while minimizing the amount of material needed. The most famous appearance is the U.S. Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal, a gleaming white hemisphere that instantly became the fair's iconic symbol.

The structure requires no interior supports or walls, as the exterior dome itself is load-bearing, creating vast open interior space. Architects and utopian thinkers were fascinated by it—geodesic domes seemed to promise an efficient, beautiful solution to shelter and community design. Modern uses range from botanical gardens and exhibition halls to off-grid homes and disaster-relief structures, still used in research stations, notably in Antarctica. Fuller called it "Spaceship Earth," a design philosophy emphasizing efficiency, sustainability, and doing more with less material—a radical vision in the nineteen fifties.

The triangular network creates exceptional rigidity, with a geodesic dome intrinsically stable and able to span vast distances without internal columns or flying buttresses. Variations exist, with domes potentially being complete spheres, hemispheres, or partial spheres, each optimized for different functions and aesthetic goals. The Montreal Expo 67 dome, also called the Biosphere, now functions as an environmental museum, cementing its place as an architectural landmark. Challenges include weather damage, with the Montreal dome's acrylic panels requiring decades of restoration, plus durability of materials and the complexity of constructing the precise triangular framework.
